summary:
I've been building Keikochō, a Japanese-learning app I use myself, and most of this month's work has been fixing subtle content bugs in a grammar engine that generates its own drill sentences. The lexicon distinguishes what a word *is* from how it renders in either language, so "this is a red" and "this is book" — broken English glosses from a fixed sentence template — get fixed once instead of patched per phrase. Building the composition layer paid off immediately: it caught that 午後十二時 actually means midnight, not noon, something the original hand-typed glosses had backwards.

A chunk of the work has been about guards that pass without checking anything. One test asserted a rule that only happened to be true at the current, smaller size of the data — it stayed green while the thing it was supposed to catch quietly stopped being caught. I've started treating a passing test as a claim to verify, not a fact, especially after data moves or a catalogue grows.

I also did a pass on Keikochō's conversational practice mode, where a bot chats back to you in Japanese. It looked fine until I actually counted: nine times out of ten, the "reply options" it offered you were four copies of the same correct answer, so there was no way to get it wrong. Same root cause as the guard problem — a de-duplication step was checking the wrong field. Fixing it meant re-grading a chunk of stored user progress rather than just shipping new code.

On the audio side, I tracked down an intermittent transcription failure that looked like a flaky network tunnel but turned out to be two services racing for the same GPU's memory at boot — whichever loaded first won, and the loser silently failed on the first real request. The fix wasn't a bigger GPU, it was pinning the allocation instead of letting it auto-size.
